Describing Persons: Level, Change, Association, and Variance

Source: vignettes/describing-persons.Rmd
describing-persons.Rmd

Person-specific analysis rests on the properties of each individual time series. Four descriptive functions are presented here. They are intended to precede model fitting, because the amount of data, the variability of each series, and the balance between stable and fluctuating variation determine which models can be estimated and how their coefficients are interpreted.

Question Function
Is each person’s series long and variable enough for analysis? describe_persons()
Which variables co-vary within each person? correlate_persons()
What share of the variance reflects stable differences between persons? variance_components()
Do correlations computed across persons describe the correlations within persons? correlate_levels()

All examples use 12 learners from the bundled srl data set, each of whom completed the same self-report items once a day, yielding 154 to 156 observations per learner.

describe_persons()

Purpose

describe_persons() returns a tidy data frame with one row for each combination of learner and variable. Two learners measured on two variables therefore yield four rows (Aisha’s efficacy, Aisha’s effort, Alice’s efficacy, Alice’s effort). The columns describe the series in each row:

  • amount of data: the number of observations (n), the number of missing values (missing), the number of days covered (span), and the typical and longest interval between consecutive observations (gap_median, gap_max);
  • level: the mean, median, minimum, and maximum;
  • variability: the standard deviation (sd), the root mean square successive difference (rmssd), and the lag-1 autocorrelation (autocor).

The two measures capture distinct properties of a series. The standard deviation (SD) quantifies the spread of observations around the person’s own mean across the full observation period. The root mean square successive difference (RMSSD) quantifies the magnitude of change between consecutive occasions. A series that drifts slowly across a wide range and a series that alternates sharply from day to day may have the same SD; the RMSSD separates the two (Jahng et al. 2008). The two quantities are related through the lag-1 autocorrelation ρ1\rho_1: for a stationary series, RMSSD≈SD2(1−ρ1)\text{RMSSD} \approx \text{SD}\sqrt{2(1-\rho_1)}.

Example 

describe_persons(analysis_data, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "effort"), time = "day", subject = c("Aisha", "Alice"))
#> PERSON DESCRIPTIVES
#>   Grouping    name
#>   Time        day
#>   People      2
#>   Variables   2
#> 
#>   subject   variable     n   miss     mean   median       sd     min       max    rmssd   autocor      span   gap_median   gap_max
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   Aisha     efficacy   156      0   56.919   61.765   21.034   0.000   100.000   26.881     0.169   155.000        1.000     1.000
#>   Alice     efficacy   156      0   35.761   36.364   20.614   0.000   100.000   28.790     0.024   155.000        1.000     1.000
#>   Aisha     effort     156      0   77.646   82.540   18.080   0.000   100.000   23.724     0.132   155.000        1.000     1.000
#>   Alice     effort     156      0   59.875   60.811   21.108   0.000   100.000   30.319    -0.032   155.000        1.000     1.000
#> 
#>   sd    = overall spread;  rmssd = occasion-to-occasion change
#>   autocor = lag-1 carry-over (inertia)

Both learners contributed 156 observations with no missing values. Mean efficacy was 57 for Aisha and 36 for Alice, whereas the SDs (21 for both) and the RMSSDs (27 and 29) were similar. The two learners therefore differed in their typical level of efficacy and showed comparable variability.

The time argument defines the chronological order of observations within each person; successive differences and autocorrelations are computed in that order. Additional columns (floor and ceiling proportions, skewness, kurtosis, linear trend, and the longest run of identical values) are returned with detail = "full".

Visualisation

plot_descriptives() displays the SD on the horizontal axis and the RMSSD on the vertical axis, with one point per person and variable.

descriptives <- describe_persons(analysis_data, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "effort"), time = "day")
plot_descriptives(descriptives)

Figure 1. Spread (SD) against day-to-day change (RMSSD) for efficacy and effort in 12 learners.

The points lie close to a straight line, with RMSSD between 1.3 and 1.5 times the SD. Under the relation given above, this ratio corresponds to small lag-1 autocorrelations: consecutive responses carried over little from one day to the next. Strong carry-over would place points well below this line.

The figure also identifies atypical learners. Erik and Eve showed the largest spread and the largest day-to-day change on both variables. Diana, Bob, and Frank showed the least variability in efficacy, while Frank’s effort was among the most variable. Stability on one variable is therefore no indication of stability on another.

Assumptions and limitations

Successive differences and autocorrelations are meaningful only when rows are ordered chronologically, so the time argument is required whenever the stored row order differs from the order of measurement. Missing occasions reduce the number of consecutive pairs available for the RMSSD and the autocorrelation. A variable that is constant within a person has an undefined correlation with any other variable and cannot serve as a predictor in that person’s model. The trend column describes a linear trend and is insensitive to abrupt shifts or other non-linear change.

correlate_persons()

Purpose

correlate_persons() estimates, separately for each person, the Pearson correlation between every pair of variables, together with a 95% confidence interval obtained through Fisher’s zz transformation. A positive within-person correlation indicates that on occasions when one variable is above that person’s typical level, the other variable also tends to be above its typical level.

Example 

correlations <- correlate_persons(analysis_data, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"), time = "day", subject = c("Aisha", "Alice"))
correlations
#> PERSON-SPECIFIC CORRELATIONS
#>   Grouping   name
#>   People     2
#>   Pairs      3
#> 
#>   subject   x            y              n        r           95% CI          p
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   Aisha     efficacy     monitoring   156    0.394     [0.25, 0.52]    < 1e-04
#>   Aisha     efficacy     effort       156    0.352     [0.21, 0.48]    < 1e-04
#>   Aisha     monitoring   effort       156    0.284     [0.13, 0.42]   0.000325
#>   Alice     efficacy     monitoring   156   -0.231   [-0.37, -0.08]   0.003736
#>   Alice     efficacy     effort       156    0.491     [0.36, 0.60]    < 1e-04
#>   Alice     monitoring   effort       156   -0.352   [-0.48, -0.21]    < 1e-04

For Aisha, all three pairs were positively correlated, with coefficients between 0.28 and 0.39. For Alice, efficacy and effort were positively correlated (0.49), whereas monitoring was negatively correlated with both efficacy (-0.23) and effort (-0.35). A single correlation computed across all learners would conceal this difference in the direction of association.

Visualisation 

plot_correlations(correlations)

Figure 2. Within-person correlations with 95% confidence intervals for two learners.

Each row corresponds to one person and one pair of variables, and rows are ordered by the size of the correlation. All six confidence intervals exclude zero.

Assumptions and limitations

The coefficients describe association between variables measured on the same occasion. Temporal precedence is examined with fit_lm() using lagged predictors or with the dynamic network models. Each coefficient is a bivariate association and is unadjusted for the remaining variables. Because consecutive daily observations are serially dependent, the confidence intervals may be too narrow. The min_n argument sets the minimum number of complete pairs required for a coefficient to be reported, and constant variables yield missing coefficients.

variance_components()

Purpose

variance_components() partitions the total variance of each variable into a between-person component, reflecting differences in person means, and a within-person component, reflecting fluctuation around each person’s mean. The intraclass correlation (ICC) is the between-person share of the total variance. Values near 0 indicate that persons have similar means and that variation arises mainly over time; values near 1 indicate stable differences between persons with little fluctuation within them.

Example 

components <- variance_components(analysis_data, vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"), id = "name")
components
#> VARIANCE COMPONENTS
#>   Grouping   name
#>   Method     anova
#> 
#>                  Within    Between     ICC   Reliability
#> --------------------------------------------------------
#>   efficacy     435.4422   290.6398   0.400         0.990
#>   monitoring   516.7891   313.4551   0.378         0.990
#>   effort       560.3849   194.4532   0.258         0.982
#> 
#>   ICC         share of variance lying BETWEEN groups
#>   Reliability precision of each group's own mean

The ICCs were 0.40 for efficacy, 0.38 for monitoring, and 0.26 for effort. Between 60% and 74% of the variance of each variable was therefore located within learners. The between-person component was nonetheless substantial. Under these conditions a regression on the raw scores combines two distinct associations: the association between a learner’s daily deviations, and the association between learners’ average levels. fit_within_between() estimates the two separately.

Visualisation 

plot_variance(components)

Figure 3. Between-person and within-person shares of variance.

Assumptions and limitations

The reliability column refers to the precision of each person’s mean and is distinct from the reliability of a single occasion. A variable that is constant within persons supports only between-person comparisons, and a variable with no between-person variation supports only within-person analysis.

correlate_levels()

Purpose

A correlation computed across persons is frequently used to describe how two variables are related within each person. Fisher, Medaglia, and Jeronimus (2018) proposed a direct test of this generalization. Two distributions of correlations are compared for the same pair of variables:

  • within persons: one correlation per person, computed across that person’s occasions;
  • between persons: one correlation per occasion, computed across persons. The first observations of all persons form one cross-sectional data set, the second observations form a second one, and so on.

When group-level results generalize to individuals, the two distributions have similar means and similar spreads. Fisher and colleagues found the within-person standard deviation to be two to four times larger than the between-person standard deviation across six samples.

Example

This example uses all 36 learners in srl, so that every between-person correlation is based on 36 persons and every within-person correlation on up to 156 occasions.

levels_result <- correlate_levels(srl, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"), time = "day")
levels_result
#> WITHIN- VERSUS BETWEEN-PERSON CORRELATIONS
#>   Grouping       name
#>   Lag adjusted   no
#> 
#>   x            y            persons   mean     SD   occasions   mean     SD   SD ratio
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   efficacy     monitoring        36   0.27   0.30         156   0.29   0.14       2.11
#>   efficacy     effort            36   0.36   0.25         156   0.50   0.14       1.82
#>   monitoring   effort            36   0.25   0.32         156   0.28   0.14       2.30
#> 
#>   within: one r per person;  between: one r per occasion
#>   SD ratio = within SD / between SD

For efficacy and monitoring, and for monitoring and effort, the mean correlations at the two levels were close (0.27 and 0.29; 0.25 and 0.28). For efficacy and effort, the mean within-person correlation (0.36) was lower than the mean between-person correlation (0.50). For all three pairs, the within-person correlations were considerably more dispersed: their standard deviation was 1.8 to 2.3 times that of the between-person correlations. For two of the three pairs, the correlation estimated across learners therefore approximated the average within-learner correlation, while the correlations of individual learners were distributed about twice as widely around that value as the between-person correlations.

Visualisation

plot_levels() displays the two distributions as density curves, following the comparison of Fisher and colleagues. Densities place the 36 within-person and 156 between-person correlations on a common scale. The ticks below each curve mark the correlations of the individual learners, and the vertical stems mark the means.

plot_levels(levels_result)

Figure 4. Distributions of within-person correlations (one per learner, solid) and between-person correlations (one per occasion, dashed) for three pairs of variables.

Temporal dependence

Serial dependence within persons can inflate the spread of within-person correlations. With lag_adjust = TRUE, each variable is first regressed on its own lag-1 value and on the lag-1 value of the other variable, and the within-person correlations are computed from the residuals.

summary(correlate_levels(srl, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"), time = "day", lag_adjust = TRUE))
#>            x          y n_within mean_within median_within sd_within n_between
#> 1   efficacy monitoring       36   0.2710705     0.2988340 0.3057933       156
#> 2   efficacy     effort       36   0.3674765     0.3562763 0.2499535       156
#> 3 monitoring     effort       36   0.2450722     0.2813312 0.3205831       156
#>   mean_between median_between sd_between mean_difference sd_ratio
#> 1    0.2873413      0.2979134  0.1446419     -0.01627083 2.114140
#> 2    0.5034717      0.5096236  0.1373181     -0.13599523 1.820251
#> 3    0.2818936      0.3080957  0.1397777     -0.03682132 2.293521

The adjustment left the results essentially unchanged: the mean within-person correlations changed by at most 0.003, and the ratios of standard deviations remained between 1.8 and 2.3. This agrees with the small lag-1 autocorrelations implied by Figure 1. The larger spread of within-person correlations is therefore attributable to differences between learners in how the variables co-vary.

Assumptions and limitations

The between-person correlations require occasions that are comparable across persons; here the tt-th observation of every learner is treated as one occasion. With fewer persons than occasions, each between-person correlation rests on a small sample, and its sampling error contributes to the between-person spread. The ratio of standard deviations is a descriptive index and is reported without a significance test.

Choice among the four functions

describe_persons() is applied first, to establish that every person has sufficient observations and variation. variance_components() then indicates whether variation is located mainly between or within persons, which determines whether the two levels must be separated in subsequent models. correlate_persons() provides an initial account of within-person co-variation, and correlate_levels() indicates how well correlations estimated across persons describe the correlations within them.

The four functions are descriptive. Models are fitted with fit_lm() for a single outcome and several predictors, with fit_within_between() for separate within-person and between-person effects, and with pool_coefs() for summarising the heterogeneity of person-specific effects.

References

Fisher, Aaron J., John D. Medaglia, and Bertus F. Jeronimus. 2018. “Lack of Group-to-Individual Generalizability Is a Threat to Human Subjects Research.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115 (27): E6106–15. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1711978115.
Jahng, Seungmin, Phillip K. Wood, and Timothy J. Trull. 2008. “Analysis of Affective Instability in Ecological Momentary Assessment: Indices Using Successive Difference and Group Comparison via Multilevel Modeling.” Psychological Methods 13 (4): 354–75. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0014173.
